title: What's running — moving across
brief: This is a phone-first page that answers one question in about a second: is anything running right now? In motion means a task an agent is working on at this moment, which is the building and verifying statuses and nothing else. On the corpus today that is four tasks and it is frequently zero, so the nearly-empty page is the state this design lives in most of the time and emptiness must read as deliberate rather than as a page that failed to load. The layout starts at roughly three hundred and seventy pixels wide and grows from there; touch targets are generous and nothing depends on hover or a pointer. The corpus is live over an SSE feed. Dark is the sole colour mode and status colour is reserved for state, never decoration. This round builds on two settled findings. The first, two rounds old and kept by every approach since: the running view has two scales, a grid of every runner at once and a single full-screen card, one control between them, and identity survives the move in both directions. The second is last round's winner, Pushed: going up is a real navigation — a release and a project are places, the browser's history owns the stack, and the phone's edge-swipe, the hardware back and the on-screen control are the same back. What this round attacks is what that winner is worst at. Watching the page in use showed a reader who does not climb once and come down; they jump around, constantly and laterally — from a task to its release, from a task in that release to a different task, from there to the project, back to the running view, out to another release — and a stack prices every lateral move as a pop followed by a push. The winner's own report conceded the edges: from the grid, going up is two taps; from the empty state there is no way up at all; and an ancestor already on the stack is rendered inert text, so the model itself forbids some jumps the reader plainly wants. The question this round asks is therefore not how to go up but how to move: how does a reader who is always in motion between task, release and project make every jump feel like one continuous, seamless act — never disoriented, never more than a tap or a gesture from where they want to be, and never in doubt about where they are and how to get back? Every approach must keep what is settled: the running view's two scales, real back behaviour that never traps the phone's edge-swipe, identity surviving every transition, and the running view still refusing to express a non-running status. The relaxation from last round stands — a release screen or listing may show its whole contents honestly, every status, with colour extended only as far as honesty requires. Each approach must also answer the two conceded edges explicitly: what going up costs from the grid, and what the empty state offers a reader who arrives when nothing runs, because a page that is usually empty and only navigable when full is a page that is usually a dead end. Motion is part of the material here — transitions must orient rather than decorate, must respect prefers-reduced-motion, and a transition that replays intermediate places the reader did not choose to revisit is the page losing their place.

approaches.title: The stack grows rails
approaches.direction: Keeps last round's winning push-stack exactly as it stands and adds the smallest thing that could dissolve its lateral cost: a persistent standing rail naming task, release and project, present on every screen including the pushed ones, so any level is one tap from anywhere and back still means what the browser says it means. Tests whether the jumping-around problem is solved by shortcuts over a stack rather than by replacing the stack, and what a permanent rail costs a 370px page that used to spend that height on content.
deviations: Every deviation recorded by Pushed (whats-running-up/u3) is inherited unchanged and not restated: the release-screen status relaxation and eight-colour map, the hash-encoded browser-owned stack, frames as siblings of PageFrame, the --space-7 touch floor over --filter-control-height, inert off-screen deck slots, the bare destination-row buttons, BackLink refused for history.back(), literal font-size ceilings above --text-lead, and the dropped Footer/PageSection/Container/PageHeader from the seeded shell.

A rail jump DOWN the stack is history.go(delta) in one call, never a sequence of pops: the browser fires one popstate for the whole distance and the page renders the stack it decodes, so no intermediate screen renders, the entries beneath the landing survive untouched, and back afterwards means exactly what it meant before. Nothing but pushState and go() ever touches history and the rail carries no touch handlers, so the phone's edge-swipe pops only places the reader actually stood.

A rail jump to somewhere NOT on the stack is one push recording where the reader actually went, never a synthesised path: from the grid, tapping the rail's release slot pushes the release directly and back returns to the grid. Inventing intermediate entries so the stack looked hierarchical would make back replay screens the reader never chose, which the brief names as the page losing their place.

The rail names the current runner's lineage — selected task, its release, its project — not the lineage of the screen on top, which names itself in its own title. The selection cannot move while a screen is pushed (the running view is inert), so the thread cannot change under the reader mid-journey. A slot naming where the reader stands renders as text marked aria-current=location: Pushed's no-forward-to-where-you-stand rule wearing the rail's clothes.

The conceded grid edge: going up from the grid is now one tap, on the rail, and the cell keeps its single action. The rail follows the grid's roving selection, so the reader aims a thumb at a permanent 48px slot rather than inside a 158px cell.

The conceded empty edge: the empty state keeps the rail at full shape, honestly empty — no task and no release exist and those slots say so — and the project slot widens to 'all projects', a new third frame kind pushing an index of every project from which projects and releases open as normal pushes. The index is name, one line, release count and nothing else: task rollups, activity and search were all refused as the corpus browser arriving through the door the empty state opened. One sentence of NothingRunning changed to say the rail still goes somewhere.

In the empty state's rail the first slot renames from Task to Running ('nothing yet'), because with no task to name the slot names the level instead — from a pushed screen the running view must still be one tap away or the rail's promise has an exception in the page's most common state.

Pushed's 'ancestor already on the stack is inert text' rule is kept verbatim on the in-screen destination rows, but the rail deliberately un-forbids those jumps: a place already beneath you is one tap to RETURN to via go(), a move down the stack rather than a growth of it. The depth bound survives (the stack still cannot cycle) while the jumps the old model forbade become the cheapest moves on the page.

What the rail costs a 370px page, measured as one number: --rail-clearance = --space-8 + --space-7 + --space-5 (136px), of which --space-8 (64px: 48px slots, 4px HERE rule, 8px breathing, border) is the rail itself and the rest is the harness pager clearance Pushed already paid, now folded inside the rail's opaque apron. Every screen clears the same property declared once on the page root, and the grid's four cells and the card's title clamp each give up that 64px of height.

The rail sits at --z-toast: it must clear the pushed screens at --z-overlay while staying under the dev chrome at --z-widget, and toast is the elevation tier the system has for a fixed strip at the bottom of the viewport. No token names 'persistent page-owned chrome above overlays'; reported as an observation rather than worked around with a raw z-index.

Breadcrumb was the library's nearest answer to the rail and is refused on three measured grounds: it is an inline <ol> of href links and a rail tap is history.go()/pushState with no document to href to; its items are single-line inline text and a rail slot is a two-line left-aligned 48px touch target; and it emits JSON-LD BreadcrumbList structured data, which would be a claim to search engines about documents that do not exist for a navigation stack that is page state.

The rail's slots and the project index's rows are bare <button> elements, both flagged raw-element by review_markup and both refused: Button is a centred pill with fixed height and its own padding, and these are full-width left-aligned multi-line columns holding 48px targets. This is the same destination-row component gap Pushed named, now needed in a third shape — the library gap is one 'destination row' primitive, not three page-local buttons.

review_markup's tailwind-shadow advisory on --font-mono (defined by Tailwind v4's default @theme as well as Alfons) is refused rather than fixed: every inherited component from the settled winner uses the token, the dev surface loads the same stylesheet stack as the catalogue where the Alfons value wins, and renaming the winner's typography to dodge an import-order hazard that does not occur on this surface would be a deviation from the inherited design, not from the hazard.

approaches.title: The map, not the stack
approaches.direction: Replaces depth with position: the corpus is a fixed spatial arrangement — projects contain releases contain tasks — and the reader pans and zooms a camera over it rather than pushing screens. A jump is the camera moving, orientation is the map itself, and back is the camera returning along where you have been. Tests whether spatial memory beats navigational memory for a reader in constant motion, and whether a map can stay legible and glanceable on a phone when the corpus is dozens of releases wide and usually almost nothing is running.
deviations: The free pan-zoom canvas the direction names is declined, deliberately: zoom is level of detail, not a CSS transform. A transform-scaled map eats the phone's scroll gesture, renders distant text unreadably small, and gives assistive technology nothing — the risks the brief itself names. Instead the pan is the page's own vertical scroll, zoom is magnification of detail (the place under the camera expands in situ, everything off its path dims and compresses to thin strips), and every camera stop — project, release, runner — is a real focusable element with a 48px target. Continuous pan survives as the scroll it always was.

The camera's hash carries ONE target (`#at/release/auth-hardening`), not the stack of frames the winning approach encoded. A camera has position, not depth: standing over a project after visiting three releases is the same place as standing over it directly, and encoding the journey would give two readers at one spot two different URLs. The journey lives in the browser's history — every deliberate move is a pushState, popstate moves the camera back, Escape calls the same back, and a deep link primes one rebuilt entry so back from a restored position lifts to the overview rather than leaving the page.

The settled running view's two scales are re-read as two camera distances, and the grid is dissolved into the map: 'All running' is the high camera — the whole corpus in frame, quiet territories as thin 48px strips so it fits roughly one screen, the runners lit in place — and 'One at a time' expands one runner into the full card where it stands. The card is no longer position:fixed and full-screen, because a fixed screen over the map would be a pushed screen, which is the thing this approach replaces. Identity survives both directions because the task never moves; only the camera does.

The card's two destination buttons are deleted. The winning card earned them because a pushed screen covered all context; on the map the release header and project header are already on screen, directly above the expanded card, and they are the camera stops. Going up from the reading position is one tap on the visible ground; from the high camera it is also one tap, because release and project headers are stops on the map itself — the two-tap grid edge the winner conceded does not exist here.

The empty state shrinks from a full-screen card to a band above the map, because a map with zero runners is not an empty page: the whole corpus is still rendered beneath it, dimmed, with nothing lit, and every project and release stop still works. The settled card's three devices (result sentence, clock time, moving beacon) are kept; EmptyState (the library atom) remains wrong for the settled reasons. This is the approach's answer to the round's dead-end edge: the page is navigable precisely when it is usual.

Sibling moves at the low camera (previous/next runner) are replaceState, not pushState, on the settled deck's precedent that paging between cards was never a history entry: back from any runner lifts the camera in one step rather than replaying every runner paged past, while the hash still updates so a reload restores the runner being read. The deck's swipe track itself is gone — runners live at fixed distant points on the map, and a horizontal scroller would be a second spatial system layered over the first. Prev/next buttons with arrow-key support in a fixed bottom rail replace it.

The eight-status colour map and its containment are inherited exactly: amber and blush mean building and verifying everywhere, and the other six colours exist only inside a release the camera has deliberately opened. Everywhere else on the map, settled work is mass — muted dots and dimmed territories rendered by opacity (--opacity-tertiary), never by status colour — so the map at running scales still refuses to express a non-running status.

Inside an honestly opened release, a running task row is a camera stop (one tap jumps release → task, the lateral move this round is about) but a settled task stays plain text, because going down was never relaxed and a done task is not a place the camera goes. Same downward line the winning release screen drew, kept under a model that made crossing it tempting.

The page is a vertically scrolling document, breaking the inherited 'exactly one screen tall' shell rule. That rule existed to keep a horizontal deck track out of a vertical scroller; there is no horizontal track here, and the scroll IS the pan. The one-line answer rides a sticky topbar instead, the headline doubling as the way home — tapping '4 running' lifts the camera to the whole map, which also gives release and project cameras a forward path home the two-segment scale control cannot offer.

When the camera stands on a place, territories off its path collapse to their head rows — including territories holding runners, whose lit chips leave the frame. Depth of field costs the page its peripheral runners while reading one; the count in each dimmed head ('· 2 running') and the fixed rail's '2 of 4' are what remain of them. Measured trade: without compression the ledger release opened honestly pushes gateway's runner ~1400px below the fold anyway, so what is lost was not legible.

Six bare <button>s flagged raw-element by review_markup and declined: territory heads, release head rows, runner nameplates, running task rows in an open release, and the headline lift. Every one is a full-width left-aligned row or an element wearing an h1, and Button is a centred pill with fixed padding — the same missing destination-row/nameplate component now reported by three approaches across two rounds. review_markup's tailwind-shadow finding on --font-mono is declined as a library-wide import-order fact, not a page defect: the dev harness loads the same stylesheet stack as the catalogue.

Inherited and re-reported unchanged: ScaleControl reaches into ToggleGroup's class names to lift 34px segments to 48px and the page's live readout stands in for the aria-pressed ToggleGroup does not emit; --filter-control-height is abandoned for --space-7 as the touch floor (2.25rem from 640px up is under 44px); literal font-size ceilings (1.75rem) above the --text-lead scale cap; the seeded Footer/PageSection/Container/PageHeader shell dropped; the fixed bottom control bar rendered outside PageFrame for the settled stacking-context reason and offset by the harness pager's clearance, which a production page would not carry.

approaches.title: The trail is the interface
approaches.direction: Makes the reader's own journey the primary navigation surface: every place visited joins a persistent trail, and the trail is rendered as a first-class strip the reader can reopen anywhere in one tap, like a hand of cards they have picked up. Jumping back is never a climb because nothing is ever behind anything else. Tests whether recency is the truest model of a reader who jumps around — whether where-I-was-just-now beats where-this-sits-in-the-hierarchy — and what happens when the trail grows past what a phone can show.
deviations: The winner's stack is replaced by one open place: a release or project screen REPLACES the screen before it rather than stacking a frame on it, so nothing is ever behind anything else and a lateral jump is priced at one tap everywhere. The stack's whole apparatus — frames array, depth-bounded-by-a-rule, ancestors rendered as inert 'open below' text — is deleted, because with no depth the release/project/release loop has nothing to grow: the browser's history records the loop honestly as the journey it was, and the trail dedupes it into one chip per place. The model now forbids no jump, which was the conceded edge this round was called to attack.

Back walks the trail. Every trail tap and every destination tap is a pushState into the location hash (inherited: the harness routes on pathname, the query carries ?empty and ?live; the hash holds ONE place now, not a stack), so the phone's edge-swipe, the hardware back and the on-screen control are one back, and it retraces the reader's own journey place by place — including revisits, because history keeps the duplicates the trail dedupes. A restored place rebuilds one entry beneath it on arrival so back from a reload goes to Running rather than out of the page.

The trail is deduped by identity with move-to-front, capped at twelve, newest at the left edge, and persisted per tab in sessionStorage. Dedupe because three copies of auth-hardening is a log answering 'what did I do' rather than 'where can I go'; the cap because past about a dozen distinct places recency has decayed to bookmarks, which are a different feature; sideways scroll for what the cap keeps so 'one tap' never hides behind a menu; sessionStorage because the trail is this reader's journey in this sitting, not a server fact, and a fresh tab honestly starts without one.

Measured cost of the strip on a 370x800 phone: the bottom reserve grows from the winner's 72px (all harness-pager clearance) to 136px — strip top padding 8, one 48px chip row, then the same 72px pager clearance folded inside the strip's own band so the dev pager floats over empty strip surface rather than over chips. The trail itself therefore costs every screen, card included, 64px; in production with no pager the whole bottom spend would be that 64px. The card survives it: the title clamp and the tightened spacing inherited from the winner already made the title give ground rather than overprint.

A trail chip is a 48px two-line plate — kind and state in mono microtype above, name below — rendered as a bare <button>. The Chip atom was checked first and refused: it is a tag token with --space-1/--space-2 padding, a remove affordance and one centred line, so every dimension of a 44px-minimum two-line navigation plate would be an override. Reported via review_markup's raw-element findings rather than worked around; it is the same gap as the winner's destination rows, which this approach also inherits (card, release screen, project screen) plus one new instance for running task rows.

A task chip whose task has ended re-points to its release and says so on its own face: the state line reads 'task · ended' and the name line reads 'AL-014 → schema-lives-here', with the tap going where the arrow points. The chip cannot reopen the running view — the running view never expresses a non-running status and the trail does not get to relax that — but a dead chip would make the trail decay into furniture exactly when the corpus empties. The visible arrow is what keeps the redirected tap an honest promise rather than a surprise.

The empty state is navigable for the first time in three rounds, and it is the trail that does it: the chips survive the corpus emptying (and a reload), so a reader who arrives when nothing runs still has every recent place one tap away, with ended task chips leading to their releases. Before anything has ever been visited the strip shows the pinned Running chip and one sentence — 'Places you open gather here, newest first.' — because a strip that only appears once used would be undiscoverable exactly when it matters, and an empty room that names its purpose reads as deliberate.

Going up from the grid: warm, one tap — any release or project already on the trail is reachable from grid scale directly, which the stack priced at two taps minimum and sometimes forbade. Cold, unchanged at two taps (open the card, then the release): a 158px grid cell still carries exactly one action, inherited reasoning, and the trail deliberately does not pre-seed places the reader never chose — a trail of unvisited places would be a sitemap wearing the trail's clothes.

Running task rows on the release screen became destinations: tapping one navigates home (a real pushState, so back returns to the release) and lands the running view at card scale on that task. This is the task-to-different-task lateral jump the round watched readers want, offered where the corpus presents it. Only building and verifying rows are tappable — there is no task screen, so a done task has nowhere to go and a control that goes nowhere is furniture; going down remains unrelaxed.

review_markup findings refused with reasons: unknown-token on --status-building/--status-verifying in TrailStrip (declared once at the page root on purpose, the winner's pattern, so eight status colours have one home); tailwind-shadow on --font-mono (present throughout the inherited winner's components; the dev harness loads the catalogue's stylesheet order, where the Alfons value wins — noted as a library-wide finding rather than restyled); raw-element on every chip and destination row (the plate component named above, which the library still does not have).

The current place's own chip stays on the strip but is disabled and border-marked rather than tappable — a hand of cards with the held card missing would misreport the hand, but offering the reader a navigation to where they stand would be the inert-ancestor problem reborn as a button. Being current is not a status, so the marking is neutral (--text-primary border), never a status colour.

Inherited unchanged from the winner, u3: the two-scale running view and its refusal of non-running statuses; status colour extended to all eight ledger labels only where a whole release is shown honestly; the release screen showing every status grouped by phase; screens rendered as siblings of PageFrame because its stacking context traps a fixed screen under the Header; --space-7 as the touch floor where --filter-control-height drops to 36px above 640px; inert off-screen deck slots; the dropped Footer/PageSection/Container shell; the literal font-size ceilings above --text-lead; and prefers-reduced-motion collapsing the place-screen slide to zero duration while the position still changes.

approaches.title: Peek, then commit
approaches.direction: Makes every jump reversible before it happens: touching a destination raises it as a partial sheet over where you stand — enough to read, cheap to dismiss — and a second act commits it to a full navigation. Most jumps in a jumping-around session are really glances, so the page prices glances at nearly nothing and full moves stay real navigations with real back. Tests whether the seamlessness the reader wants is actually cheap reversibility rather than fast travel, and whether a two-stage gesture can be discoverable and honest on a touch screen without hover.
deviations: Modal is not used for the peek sheet, and that is the library gap this approach exists to expose: Modal is a centred scale-in dialog, it is styled entirely with --admin-* tokens on what is a public surface, it sits at --z-overlay (which u4 measured losing to the Header at --z-widget), and it has no way to carry a pinned commit bar, a swipe-down grip or a partial height. A local PeekSheet replaces it. The finding is that the library has a confirmation dialog and no application sheet.

A peek IS a history entry — one, however far the glance wanders. In history, because a sheet outside it means the phone's edge-swipe made under a sheet leaves the page entirely, the same trap u3 named for an in-page stack; only one, because swapping the peeked subject (release to its project, project to another release) is a replaceState, so a whole chain of glances is put down by a single back and never becomes places back must replay — the brief's 'replaying intermediate places' failure, priced out by construction.

Committing rewrites the peek entry rather than stacking on it: after commit, history reads [running, release] as if the reader had navigated directly, so back from a committed place never revisits the glance that led there. A reloaded URL carrying a peek is likewise rewritten to its committed stack — a glance is ephemeral by definition and has no opener to return focus to.

u3's inert-text rule for an already-open ancestor is replaced: any frame can be peeked, and the sheet's commit control becomes 'Return to …', implemented as history.go backwards to the existing entry. The stack stays bounded (release/project/release can never grow) without the model forbidding a jump the round brief says the reader plainly wants, and nothing renders as a control-shaped non-control.

The grid cell gains a second target, departing from the two-rounds-settled 'a cell is a nameplate with one action': the where block (project + release) is now a 48px peek button with a 'peek' cue. Reasoned from the approach's own thesis — a full navigation would fight the cell's one job, but a glance is cheap enough for a 158px cell to afford — and it answers the two-taps-from-the-grid concession: one tap now reads a release from the landing state. The cost is stated: the plate gives up two of its six rows to keep the peek row at 44px.

The empty state offers the corpus's releases as peek rows below the unchanged statement, so the page's usual state stops being its only dead end. What that admits is recorded rather than hidden: the moment the empty state lists releases, the page has a second job — glancing at the corpus — independent of anything running. The list is kept subordinate (statement keeps the display type, rows are small) and carries no status colour, because nothing there is running.

Every destination tap on the page now peeks rather than navigates, and each destination row carries a mono 'peek' cue where u3 had a bare chevron — a two-stage gesture that hides its first stage is a lie about cost, and the cue plus the sheet's fully-named commit control ('Go to release schema-lives-here', never 'Open') is how the two stages stay discoverable on a touch screen without hover and without any long-press.

The sheet is modal to the keyboard without a hand-rolled focus trap: role=dialog, aria-modal, and inert on everything beneath (the running view and every committed frame) is the whole fence. The scrim is aria-hidden and out of the tab order — Escape and the labelled Close button are the keyboard's exits, all routed through the same history.back() as the swipe-down and the phone's own back. Focus re-lands on the dialog region when a swap changes its subject, because a sheet that silently becomes a different release has lost a screen reader.

Layering, inherited from measurement not taste: committed screens are siblings of PageFrame at --z-overlay (u3 measured the wordmark intercepting the back control when a fixed screen rendered inside the shell's stacking context), and the sheet and scrim sit at --z-widget (u4 measured a sheet at --z-overlay being modal to the keyboard yet walked around by a mouse, because the Header is --z-widget). --z-widget incidentally also keeps a peek raised from a committed screen above that screen.

The sheet is centred above 640px by margin-inline, never by transform: the rise transition and the swipe-down both write transform, and a translateX(-50%) centring would be overwritten mid-animation, snapping the sheet sideways. Reasoned from reading the transition contract, then kept as a rule.

Inherited from u3 and unchanged, restated because they still bind: the release content renders all eight ledger statuses (a release shown as only its runners is a lie about the release) with status colour extended exactly that far and only the two motion statuses breathing; the seeded shell's Footer, PageSection, Container and PageHeader are dropped because the running view is exactly one screen tall; off-screen deck slots are inert; padding-bottom on the running view, every pushed screen and the sheet's commit bar clears the harness's floating pager; and --filter-control-height is refused as a touch floor in favour of --space-7, because it resolves to 36-41px from 640px up.

Bare <button> elements throughout, all flagged raw-element and all refused for u3's reason: Button is a centred pill with fixed padding, and a full-width row — rank/name/cue destination, grid plate, cell where-row, project release row, empty-state release row — is a Button in name only. The missing component is now needed in five distinct places plus a cue variant; promoting the winner without absorbing a 'destination row' atom would recreate this finding a fourth round running.

review_markup's unknown-token findings on --status-building/--status-verifying in TaskCell are refused: the eight --status-* properties are declared once at the page root and resolved in child components, which the per-component rule cannot see. Declaring them per component would trade one advisory finding for eight copies of the palette.

review_markup's tailwind-shadow finding on --font-mono (fires in every file that sets it) is refused: the dev harness loads the same stylesheet stack and order as the catalogue, where the Alfons value wins, and the token is used identically across the whole prototype corpus — a prototype is the wrong place to relitigate the library's import order. Reported rather than worked around.

Literal font-size ceilings in clamps survive from every prior approach and gain one: 1.75rem on the page headline and the empty statement (stepped down from u3's 2.125rem to buy the glance list its height), 2.125rem on the card title, and 1.5rem on the sheet's subject name. The floor is a token every time; the public scale still stops at --text-lead, which is a caption size for the name of the thing being peeked.

approaches.title: One surface, two axes
approaches.direction: Collapses the hierarchy into a single continuous surface with two axes: vertical moves change level — task up to release up to project — and horizontal moves walk siblings at the level you are on. There are no pushed screens and no overlays; the page is one navigable space and the reader is always somewhere on it, with position echoed by a persistent two-axis indicator. Tests whether a consistent gesture grammar can make dozens of possible jumps feel like one instrument, and whether axis navigation can coexist with the deck's existing horizontal swipe without the two gestures fighting.
deviations: The winner's card loses its two destination buttons, and the 'where' line returns as plain text. Why: the vertical axis is one persistent control that works from every state of every level, and a per-card copy of the same move would be the page offering one jump in two grammars. The card gets back the 128px u3 measured the destination rows costing its title, and the collision at the heart of this approach dissolves by adoption — the deck's settled swipe simply IS the horizontal axis at task level, unchanged.

The deck's off-screen slots are exposed again, reversing u3's inert. Why: u3 made them inert because every card carried two buttons and a reader tabbing off card one landed on card three's release. With the cards control-free the two-scale winner's original reasoning stands again — four cards read end to end beats one card plus a gesture. PanelTrack's slots ARE inert, because a release panel is full of controls and vertically scrollable text.

Vertical is buttons only; swipe-vertical is not implemented even as the enhancement the direction invited. Why: the one-screen page has no page scroll to fight, but the release and project panels must scroll vertically — a release is a list of a length the corpus decides — so a vertical gesture already means something on two of the three levels, and a gesture that changes level over the task pane but scrolls a list one pane up is a grammar that lies. The axis pair is 48px each and present in every state, including empty.

History: vertical moves push, horizontal moves replace, and both directions of the vertical axis push. Why: back that replays twelve sibling swipes in reverse is a back button that has stopped working; a level change is a decision, a swipe is a glance. replaceState keeps each entry's URL current, so back lands on the level below at the exact sibling the reader was reading when they climbed. Down is a push rather than history.back() because an undo that sometimes rewinds through positions the reader never meant to revisit is worse than a longer history.

A reloaded deep position gets no synthetic history entries beneath it, departing from u3, which rebuilt its stack on restore. Why: a stack claims frames exist beneath you; a position claims nothing. Back from a freshly loaded #project/ledger leaves the page, which is the browser telling the truth about this session — and the down control is standing right there. Escape maps to history.back() only while a session-pushed entry survives, so it never throws the reader out of the page.

The conceded edges answered: from the grid, going up is ONE tap — the axis bar is persistent and anchors to the selected cell — where the stack priced it at two; and the empty state keeps its whole way up, because the axis exists independently of what the task level contains. Up from the empty task level lands on the remembered (or first) release, and NothingRunning's reassurance line now names the affordance.

Down from a release re-anchors only when the release holds a runner (landing on that runner, at card scale when reached by a panel row's dive); a release with no runner descends to the running view exactly as the reader left it, and the control names that honestly — the runner's id, 'the running view', or 'nothing running'. A project with no releases disables down: an honest floor, not a broken lift.

BREACH carried from last round, re-recorded: the release level renders every ledger status and status colour extends to all eight labels. Amber and blush still mean building and verifying and nothing else; the task level's types (RunningStatus narrower than TaskStatus) still make a non-running status inexpressible in the grid and deck. u5's two devices are inherited: only motion statuses animate, and settled tasks render at --opacity-tertiary, so the one runner in a release of six is the only thing at full strength.

The axis buttons print the destination's name, not its kind — 'auth-hardening', never 'RELEASE · UP'. Why: u1 measured the collision at 370px (each half of a split bar is ~150px and kind-plus-slug wraps then truncates the slug); the kind lives in the chevron and the aria-label. The aria-hidden two-axis indicator between them echoes level and sibling index, with the page's single live readout speaking the same fact so two voices never overlap.

PanelTrack duplicates the deck's snap-track mechanics (instant first positioning, the settling flag, roving tick focus) rather than reusing TaskDeck. Reported as the library gap it is: Alfons has no snap-pager primitive, and this is now the third round to rebuild one. The one structural difference is load-bearing — deck slots clip both axes to protect the swipe; panel slots scroll vertically.

Bare <button> elements throughout — the axis bar's two rung buttons, the release panels' runner rows, the project panels' release rows, and both rails' ticks — all flagged raw-element and declined. Button is a centred pill with fixed padding; a destination row (rank/name/chevron filling the width at a 48px floor) is the same missing component three rounds have now reported, and a 48px hit area around a 4px bar is exactly what Button's styling would have to be removed to build.

--filter-control-height is not used as the touch floor anywhere; --space-7 carries every target (axis buttons, runner rows, release rows, ticks, ScaleControl's segments). Why: measured last round — the token drops to 2.25rem from 640px up, under 44px exactly where a touchscreen laptop reads this page. ScaleControl still reaches :global into ToggleGroup to lift its 34px segments, re-reported unchanged.

review_markup's tailwind-shadow finding on --font-mono (nine sites) is declined: the dev harness loads the catalogue's stylesheet stack in production order, where the Alfons value wins, and every sibling approach and half the library spell it the same way. Its unknown-token finding on --offset was taken in spirit: the property is set from markup per pane, which the rule cannot see, so a default '--offset: 0' now lives in the style block — reported as a rule limit: a custom property set only via a style attribute reads as unresolved.

Icon has no arrow-up/arrow-down; the axis pair wears chevron-up/chevron-down while the horizontal rails keep arrow-left/arrow-right. Reported as a small asymmetry in the icon set: the vertical axis cannot match the horizontal one's vocabulary.

Inherited from the winning approach and re-recorded: the seeded shell's Footer, PageSection, Container and PageHeader are dropped (the page is exactly one screen tall so the surface never fights a document scroll); padding-bottom is calc(var(--space-7) + var(--space-5)) to clear the harness's floating pager; literal font-size ceilings in the clamps (1.75rem on the headline and panel names, 2.125rem on the card title and empty statement) because the public type scale stops at --text-lead; and Pill wears fill='soft' tint='var(--text-muted)' because its canonical warm tint sits beside amber, which means building here.

The page's h1 answers the page's one question from every level — it stays '4 running' while the reader stands three projects away, and the panel under them names the place. Position and answer are two different facts held apart, which is what lets the brief's one-second read survive the reader being anywhere on the surface.
